newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Council-Parliament set for television shootout.
newsitem.headline: Council-Parliament set for television shootout.

text.p: The Culture Council and the European Parliament seem destined for a Wild-West style showdown next month over plans to revise the 1989 Television without Frontiers directive.

The parliament's Culture Committee made confrontation more likely this week when it maintained calls for stricter limits -- opposed by EU capitals -- on the number of Hollywood films and programmes shown on the EU's television screens.

If the full parliament follows the Committee's advice in its second reading in Strasbourg on November 13 -- and that could prove to be the unknown twist in the tale -- there could be a bloody climax to one of the EU's most protracted sagas.
The issue would go to "conciliation", when both sides go to the negotiating table and seek to hammer out their differences.

On the surface the question is how to revise the EU's 1989 directive -- 89/552/EEC (COM(96)200 -- which said that television stations should, but only "where practicable", devote 51 percent of their screen time to European productions.

The parliament, aware that the EU's film industry is struggling, and under intense lobbying by French filmmakers, wants that provision made mandatory. Under the committee's recommendation for the parliament's second reading member states would have to enforce the quota by legal means.
The Culture Council, on the other hand, believes that tougher quotas are not the answer and agreed to leave the 1989 directive exactly as it is.
But it is not just a question of cinema.
Underlying the storyline is the European Parliament's desire to be taken more seriously and have the new co-decision powers it received under the Maastricht Treaty actually amount to something.
The parliament has taken the Council's rejection of its position as a slap in the face.
As in many films it might be possible to predict the ending -- regardless of who are the goodies or the baddies -- and the parliament is a certain loser in the shoot out.
If the issue goes to conciliation and the two sides fail to agree, the directive will remain as it is -- exactly what the Council wants.

For that reason, EU officials say, some deputies might, when it comes to the vote next month, prefer to avoid a showdown to avoid an inevitable defeat and abandon the Culture Committee line and its Chairwoman Luciana Castellina.
"The whole question is -- will the parliament follow Castellina. It is impossible at this stage to predict," said one EU official.
The Culture Committee has also departed from the Council position in demanding a tougher defintion of broadcasting, to include video on demand, but not the internet.
It wants tougher rules for advertising and teleshopping, saying advertising should last for no longer than 15 percent of the film's duration.

The Committee also wants rules to ensure that broadcasters who receive exclusive rights to screen important sports events like the Olympic Games or the football World Cup do not prevent people from following the events live.
